prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first and the lattice clock third, but after reading all eight ballots I move B052 to the top of my configuration. It is the only candidate that every member ranked, with two first places and four top-three placements, and no colleague raised a scientific objection to it; the reservations are about overlap with earlier prizes, not about the result. As an instrument builder I judge it on the criteria I use for my own field: a new measurement technique that changes what can be observed, independent reproduction, and a clear credited contribution. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removed the Stark-shift limit on many-atom interrogation, and Ye's group took the clocks to uncertainties near 1e-18. Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) now compare lattice clocks at that level, and they feed relativistic geodesy, fundamental-constant and dark-matter searches, and the redefinition of the second. The two-name attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, which matters because the statutes cap us at three people. As Chair I also note that this is the one candidate around which the committee can plausibly converge without anyone having to suppress a scientific concern.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that metrology of this kind can be read as a refinement of the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize rather than a discovery in its own right, and the pending redefinition of the second means its practical culmination is still ahead. Attribution is clean at the level of the two principal names but not absolute: the Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and ion-clock groups have credible claims to part of the narrative, and I cannot verify every priority claim from the provided material. Atomic physics is also outside my own expertise, so I am relying on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson for how this ranks scientifically against atom interferometry and against other metrology. If the committee decides it wants a discovery of nature rather than a new instrument, IceCube (B043) is my alternative.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B052 first as the clearest case of a new measurement technique changing what can be observed, with breadth of consequence from geodesy to a candidate redefinition of the second, and as a natural successor to the 2005 comb prize and earlier precision-spectroscopy prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the criterion and, from the instrument side, with the conclusion. Your point about independent comparison over fibre links is what persuades me most: that is exactly the independent confirmation I ask for. Where I differ slightly is B035. You rank atom interferometry second, but your own ballot concedes that Chu's absence and the 1997 and 2001 overlap make the three-way split hard, and the most dramatic applications are still undemonstrated. I would keep B035 as an alternative, not as a partner to B052.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B052 first as clean, original and fundamental, and asked whether the committee would see it as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize. She also ranked B035 second and B044 fourth, flagging that excluding Zoller and Jaksch from B044 is a fairness problem.
responses.response: I take the overlap question seriously, and it is the main reason I list it as my strongest reservation. My answer is that the comb provided a tool and the lattice clock provides a new clock architecture: trapping many atoms at a magic wavelength so that neither motion nor the trap shifts the transition. That is a separate, decisive idea with its own priority and its own demonstration. I also agree with your point on B044: because credit for the theory proposal and the experiments cannot be split fairly in three names, I do not put it in my configuration.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked the Higgs experimental discovery (B010) first as the clearest discovery delivered by nature, while acknowledging that founder-level credit to Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee imperfectly represents collaborations of thousands. He ranked IceCube second and the lattice clock fourth.
responses.response: I share your view of the Higgs discovery as scientifically overdue, and as a collaboration member myself I know how distributed the real credit is. That is precisely why I cannot support B010 as a person-based prize: your own ballot says the decisive contributions were spread across spokespersons, trigger and analysis leaders and detector builders, and Olsson and Mehlig make the same point. I would want a configuration that survives the objection that leadership is not the same as the discovery. On IceCube, which we both ranked high, I accept your point that Halzen and Spiering form a workable pair, but source identification is still developing, so I do not think B043 is ahead of the lattice clock now.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B024) first as a clean model-meets-experiment case with large downstream impact, while noting that the superconducting mechanism is unsettled and that credit beyond the three names is contested. He ranked B052 eighth.
responses.response: I find the theory-meets-experiment pattern compelling and I ranked B024 sixth, so I do not dismiss it. But condensed matter is outside my expertise and I defer to you and Eriksson on the physics. My difficulty is maturity: you, Eriksson and Olsson all say the pairing mechanism and sample variability are unresolved, and the experiments are only eight years old. I would put the lattice clock ahead on maturity and attribution. I would like to hear in round 2 why you rank B052 so low, since your own ballot calls the magic-wavelength idea simple, general and experimentally decisive.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked topological insulators (B021) first as a verified new state of matter in real materials, but he acknowledged that the crowded attribution (Bernevig, Zhang, Fu, Hasan and others) leaves some claims unaddressed. He ranked B052 fifth, partly worried it may be seen as precision engineering over new physics.
responses.response: I respect the argument that a verified state of matter is the strongest kind of discovery, but your own attribution paragraph, and those of Lindroth, Mehlig and Olsson, show that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would leave out the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D experiments. I do not want to fix a prize that will be seen as leaving out decisive contributors. On your concern about engineering over new physics: a clock at 1e-18 is also a probe of gravitational redshift across millimetres and of variation of constants, so it does produce new physics. Your note that a thorium clock could compete for Ye's slot is a fair point that I address in the uncertainties.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B056) first and the lattice clock second, calling the clock physics clean, quantitative and controlled, with no serious dispute over the principal credit. He also flagged his own possible conflict on B056 and the closeness of the 2025 circuit prize.
responses.response: Your second-place ranking of B052 and your statement that there is no serious dispute over credit is exactly the support I need to put it forward. On B056, I appreciate your candour about your own position and I agree that a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025, and with Blais left out of a three-person split, is a hard case. I cannot judge the 2004 priority record and would rely on you and Lindroth for it, but I do not think we should resolve this in a way that leans on a member who has declared an interest.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize.
How to describe Ye's contribution so that it does not double count with a possible later nuclear-clock recognition, which is outside this shortlist.

Whether other lattice-clock groups (for example Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto) or ion-clock pioneers have priority claims strong enough to alter the two-name configuration; I cannot verify this from the provided material.
Whether the committee should instead award a discovery of nature (IceCube, B043) in a two-part prize; that would require trimming the credited names to keep the total at three people.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B052 (Katori, Ye): I have no recorded connection to either laureate or to their institutions. For B043 (IceCube) and B041 (EHT) I am a fellow experimental astroparticle and astrophysics researcher in the same broad community, though my profile lists no collaboration with those teams, and my work is in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur. I flag this field proximity for transparency only.
